entry.title: Machine Operator — Prima PMI
entry.content:
In October 2025, I joined Prima PMI in Melbourne as a Machine Operator (Christmas Casual).
During the peak production season, I worked across three departments — Calender, Guillotine (Cut Finishing), and Shipping, supporting high-volume manufacturing and fulfilment operations.

This role was my first experience in a full-scale industrial production environment, where I learned the importance of precision, adaptability, safety, and teamwork in keeping operations running efficiently under time pressure.

🏭 Calender Department (Primary Role)

The Calender Department handles punching, drilling, tabbing, and finishing processes for a wide range of paper-based products.
I spent most of my shifts here, supporting both mainline production and specialised finishing tasks.

🔹 Renz Inline 500 — Main Production Machine

High-volume punching & binding system

🔗 View official product page →

My involvement:

  • Assisted with continuous high-volume production runs
  • Material feeding, alignment checks, and output monitoring
  • Ensured punch consistency and workflow stability
  • Performed routine cleaning and basic maintenance during shift changes

This machine formed the backbone of daily calender production and required constant attention to maintain speed and quality.

🔹 Renz AP 360 Digital — Punching (Specialised Jobs)

Digital punching for customised product requirements

🔗 View official product page →

My involvement:

  • Assisted with setup for customised punching jobs
  • Adjusted material positioning based on job specifications
  • Checked punch accuracy and hole alignment
  • Supported changeovers between different product types

Used for more precise or smaller-batch punching compared to the Inline 500.

🔹 Uchida VS-20 — Paper Drilling Machine

Precision drilling for paper products

🔗 View distributor product page →

My involvement:

  • Assisted with paper positioning and drilling accuracy
  • Monitored hole consistency across batches
  • Helped with drill-bit checks and cleaning
  • Ensured safe operation during repetitive drilling tasks

This role required high attention to detail, as drilling errors could affect entire batches.

🔹 Uchida Countron — Tabbing Machine

Automatic tabbing and finishing

::contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}

🔗 Learn more about Uchida finishing equipment →

My involvement:

  • Assisted with setup and tab placement alignment
  • Monitored tab consistency and adhesion
  • Supported material handling and output collection
  • Performed basic cleaning and jam clearing

Often used at later finishing stages where visual quality was critical.

✂️ Guillotine Department (Cut Finishing)

In the Guillotine Department, I supported cut finishing for paper-based products across various production jobs.

Key responsibilities:

  • Assisting with guillotine cutting operations
  • Preparing stacks and materials for accurate cutting
  • Checking measurements and alignment before and after cuts
  • Handling finished products and preparing them for downstream processes
  • Maintaining cleanliness and safety around cutting equipment

This role reinforced the importance of precision and safety, as small errors could impact large production batches.

📦 Shipping Department

In the Shipping Department, I supported the final stage of the production pipeline — fulfilment and dispatch.

Key responsibilities:

  • Preparing finished products for shipment
  • Ensuring correct labelling, packing, and documentation
  • Verifying orders using RF scanning systems
  • Coordinating with team members to meet dispatch deadlines
  • Supporting loading and movement of outgoing goods

This role gave me visibility into how production outputs connect directly to customer delivery.

🔄 Understanding End-to-End Production Workflow

Working across Calender → Guillotine → Shipping allowed me to understand the full production lifecycle.

Key learnings:

  • Early-stage quality control prevents downstream rework
  • Clear communication between departments avoids bottlenecks
  • Timing and preparation are as important as speed
  • Small delays can impact the entire workflow

This experience strengthened my operational awareness and process mindset.

🔧 Maintenance & Machine Care

In addition to machine operation, I regularly supported basic maintenance tasks across departments:

  • Cleaning machine components and work areas
  • Clearing paper jams safely
  • Preparing machines for the next production run
  • Identifying minor issues early to minimise downtime

This hands-on exposure helped me build strong safety awareness and respect for machine care.

🧠 Skills I Developed

  • Industrial machine assistance and basic maintenance
  • Quality control and attention to detail
  • RF scanning and inventory handling
  • Workflow awareness in production environments
  • Physical endurance and safe material handling
  • Team communication in shift-based operations
  • Adaptability under high-volume, time-sensitive conditions

These skills are transferable to roles in manufacturing, print finishing, logistics, warehousing, and operations.

💭 Reflection

“Working at Prima PMI taught me that even on fast-paced production floors, consistency, teamwork, and adaptability matter just as much as technical skill.”

This experience gave me a deeper appreciation for how products are produced, finished, and delivered behind the scenes, and strengthened my discipline, work ethic, and operational mindset.
entry.summary: My experience working as a Machine Operator (Christmas Casual) at Prima PMI, where I supported production across the Calender, Guillotine (cut finishing), and Shipping departments, assisted with industrial machinery, performed basic maintenance, and ensured workflow quality during peak season.

entry.title: Pet Sitter — Camp Paws
entry.content:
I joined Camp Paws in Melbourne because I have always loved animals. I missed my pets back home and wanted to do something that let me reconnect with that sense of care. Working as a pet sitter was also a way for me to improve my communication skills and learn to handle responsibility in new environments.

🐾 Starting Out

Camp Paws did not have a physical office. Everything was managed through WhatsApp and a specialized application. I applied for several assignments when I first joined, but many were rejected. Some clients preferred sitters with more experience or longer availability. At first, it was disappointing, but I learned to approach each rejection as a chance to improve. I refined how I introduced myself, how I communicated reliability, and how I described my previous experience with animals.

Eventually, I began to receive more trust from clients. The first few visits were careful and quiet. I entered other people’s homes, followed instructions precisely, and took time to understand each dog’s habits. I learned to be patient and consistent, especially with animals that took time to warm up to new people.

🐶 The Dogs I Remember Most

Among the many dogs I cared for, three stand out in my memory: Ivy, Ziggy, and Kreuzer.
Ivy was gentle and alert, always watching before coming close. Ziggy liked to follow routines and noticed every small change. Kreuzer was strong and playful, but needed calm handling when walking outdoors. They each taught me something different about care and observation.

Through them, I learned that trust is not something that can be rushed. It is built through quiet repetition, small gestures, and consistent presence. These lessons stayed with me long after each visit ended.

✨ Lessons Learned

Working as a pet sitter was not only about caring for animals. It was about developing patience and empathy in practical ways. I learned that communication is more than what is spoken. Dogs respond to tone, energy, and rhythm. The way I moved or reacted could change how they behaved. This awareness also improved how I interacted with clients, helping me communicate clearly and respectfully.

The rejections I faced at the beginning reminded me to be humble and persistent. Over time, I learned that responsibility grows not just from experience but from reliability and genuine care.

💭 Reflection

This experience reminded me of my dogs back home, all those moment I used to have with them, and how much those memories meant to me. Being around Ivy, Ziggy, and Kreuzer gave me a sense of home in a different country. It helped me appreciate the simple value of care such as showing up on time, keeping promises, and being patient when things do not go as planned.

“Pet sitting taught me that trust—like care—grows slowly through quiet presence and genuine consistency.”
entry.summary: My experience as a freelance pet sitter with Camp Paws in Melbourne, visiting clients’ homes to care for their dogs, facing early rejections, and learning patience and empathy through every visit.

entry.title: CSER: Context-Sensitive Emotion Recognition Framework using Visual and Textual Features

link.title: CSER: Context-Sensitive Emotion Recognition Framework using Visual and Textual Features

entry.content:
This project was one of the hardest and most technically demanding research works I have ever completed.
The paper, CSER: Context-Sensitive Emotion Recognition Framework using Visual and Textual Features, introduces a multimodal system that include both Vision Transformers (ViT) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) , specifically LLaVA and BLIP to improve emotion recognition in complex, real-world settings.
This research was written in collaboration with Dr. Thuseethan Selvarajah, Prof. Sutharshan Rajasegarar, and Prof. John Yearwood all from various different institute, and submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia.

💡 Motivation

Most emotion recognition models focus on a single modality such as facial expressions or voice.
In contrast, human emotion is shaped by context which can be summarised from the surrounding scene, body posture, and situation.
The goal of CSER was to make emotion recognition context-aware, closing in the gap between how AI systems interpret emotions and how humans perceive them.

⚙️ Technical Summary

CSER combines three ViT-based visual learners for face, body, and scene with textual embeddings generated by LLaVA and BLIP.
All modalities are projected into a shared latent space and fused using multi-head and self-attention mechanisms.

Results:

  • Achieved mAP = 40.49% on EMOTIC
  • Achieved mAP = 54.28% on HECO
  • Outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods on both datasets
  • Showed major gains in subtle emotions such as sadness, fear, and embarrassment

🧠 The Hard Part

This project required months of experimentation, dataset preparation, and a lot of set backs.

Dataset scarcity:
Finding group or context-sensitive emotion datasets was nearly impossible. EMOTIC and HECO were the only usable ones as they are available and their authors can be contacted, but both had fragmented labels and inconsistent annotations that needed remapping.

Data quality issues:
Many images contained occluded faces, low light, or incomplete subjects.
To maintain uniform input shapes, I had to implement fallback logic that replaced missing faces with zero matrices which is a bit tedious but necessary step to keep the training pipeline stable.

Hardware constraints:
All experiments initially ran on a GTX 1660 Ti, forcing constant trade-offs between batch size, learning rate, and runtime stability.
Training large vision-language models pushed the limits of available memory, often causing crashes mid-run.
To overcome this, I used external GPU resources provided by Deakin University’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s compute credits.
Setting up the remote GPU environments took significant effort such as configuring CUDA, aligning PyTorch versions, and establishing secure connections, however it was essential to complete the experiments at full scale.

VLM integration:
LLaVA and BLIP produced embeddings with incompatible dimensions and token structures.
Aligning and projecting them into a shared feature space was one of the most complex implementation challenges.

Every part from data cleaning to writing tested both patience and my problem-solving skill.

💭 Reflection

Despite the obstacles, completing CSER taught me what true research persistence feels like.
It was a lesson in problem-solving under constraint, working with incomplete datasets, limited hardware, and long iteration cycles, yet still producing a model that achieved measurable progress.

Being the youngest member in the author list, I handled most of the experimental setup, ablation design, and manuscript drafting.
This experience taught me to think beyond implementation, also to question design decisions, justify model behavior, and communicate results in a professional manner.

It reminded me that scientific progress is not just about accuracy, it’s about the discipline to keep iterating when nothing seems to work.

📑 Citation

Ignasius, A., Selvarajah, T., Rajasegarar, S., & Yearwood, J. (2025).
CSER: Context-Sensitive Emotion Recognition Framework using Visual and Textual Features.
IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (Under Review).

🏷 Keywords

Emotion Recognition · Multimodal Learning · Vision Transformer · Vision-Language Models · Affective Computing

“CSER reminded me that innovation often begins where comfort ends, when you keep refining ideas long after the models stop cooperating.”
entry.summary: Reflection on developing the CSER framework — a context-sensitive emotion recognition model combining Vision Transformers and Vision-Language Models, and the challenges faced during research and dataset curation.

entry.title: Smart Recycling — Waste Classification
entry.content:
I implemented a computer-vision system that classifies household waste photos into Australia’s three-bin scheme:
Red (general), Green (organics), and Yellow (recyclables) — using the RealWaste dataset.

🧩 Problem & Dataset

  • Task: Image → {Red, Green, Yellow} bin label to help reduce recycling contamination.
  • Dataset: RealWaste (Kaggle) (materials like Cardboard, Glass, Metal, Plastic, Food Organics, etc.), remapped to 3 bins.
  • Split: ~80/10/10 train/val/test after regrouping images into bin folders.


Sample images and distribution from the training dataset.

⚙️ Approach

  • Baseline model: Small CNN (“WasteNet”), CrossEntropy, Adam, 50 epochs; track Accuracy, F1, Recall, Precision.
  • Data augmentation: resize + random flip/rotation + color jitter; normalisation with ImageNet stats; applied to train only.
  • Profiling: Compared plain vs augmented input pipelines; identified loader/CPU transforms as bottleneck; sped up with num_workers=4.
  • Equal-time study: Trained “plain” vs “augmented” under the same one-hour budget to compare generalisation.
  • Generalisation (D-task): Collected a new test set from different sources (phone/web) and built an improved CNN with BN/Dropout/Pooling.


Result on baseline (plain) model — accuracy and F1 on validation set.

📊 Results (highlights)

Setup Test Acc F1 Notes
Baseline (no augmentation) 69.5% 0.44 —
With augmentation (equal time) 70.6% 0.47 Better recall/F1
Improved (BN/Dropout/Pooling) 82.98% 0.71 On original test set
New domain test — old model ~55% — Phone/web images
New domain test — improved model ~70% — Higher F1/recall, robust

Approximate values marked with “~”.


Improved model showing higher F1 and better domain robustness.

🧠 What I Learned

  • Balanced recall/F1 matters more than raw accuracy for waste sorting (missing positives is costly).
  • Augmentation helps generalisation but must be profiled/tuned; parallel data loading reduced pipeline time ~5×–6×.
  • Architectural tweaks (BN, Dropout, Pooling) significantly improved robustness across domains.

🧰 Tech Stack

  • PyTorch, TorchVision, TensorBoard, PyTorch Profiler, scikit-learn metrics.
  • Trained on GPU where available.

“It shows how data and design can work together to make sustainability practical, one correctly sorted bin at a time.”
entry.summary: Built a bin-type image classifier (Red/Green/Yellow) with PyTorch, augmentation, profiling, and domain generalisation experiments. Includes reproducible notebook output and report PDFs.

entry.title: 3D Reconstruction with KinectFusion
entry.content:
This project was completed for SIT789: Robotics, Computer Vision, and Speech Processing at Deakin University.
The objective was to experiment with the KinectFusion algorithm for real-time 3D reconstruction using RGB-D data from the TUM dataset.
The task focused on executing a published implementation, measuring reconstruction accuracy, and analyzing limitations under different environmental complexities.

🎯 Objective

The goal was to:

  1. Implement and execute the KinectFusion algorithm on local hardware.
  2. Reconstruct 3D scenes from multiple TUM RGB-D sequences.
  3. Record performance metrics — processing time, FPS, and RMSE.
  4. Analyze how scene complexity affects reconstruction accuracy.

⚙️ Implementation

The Python-based KinectFusion repository was used from
https://github.com/JingwenWang95/KinectFusion

All dependencies were installed in an isolated environment to prevent package conflicts.

Configuration files were manually updated for each TUM dataset sequence under the configs/ directory.
Example command for reconstruction:

Resulting .ply meshes were visualized using the Open3D viewer or via
ImageToSTL 3D viewer.

🧩 Hardware Setup

  • CPU: Intel® Core™ i7-10750H (2.60 GHz)
  • GPU: NVIDIA® GeForce GTX 1660 Ti
  • Memory: 32 GB RAM

This configuration was capable of handling dense depth fusion but did not reach real-time frame rates.
Each sequence required several minutes of processing depending on scene complexity and voxel resolution.

🖼️ Reconstruction Samples

Below are the visual reconstructions generated from the TUM RGB-D sequences.

FR1_RPY — Simple Scene

*Reconstruction of FR1_RPY from two viewing angles showing stable mesh and consistent alignment.*

FR1_Room — Complex Scene

*Reconstruction of FR1_Room showing surface noise and polygon loss due to scene clutter and lighting variation.*

📈 Experimental Results

Dataset: FR1_RPY

  • Average processing time: 0.132 s / frame
  • Frame rate: 7.55 FPS
  • RMSE: 0.064 m
  • Observation: Reconstruction accuracy was high; only minor missing polygons in localized regions.

Dataset: FR1_Room

  • Average processing time: 0.158 s / frame
  • Frame rate: 6.35 FPS
  • RMSE: 0.267 m
  • Observation: Reconstruction degraded in complex indoor environments; polygon loss and surface noise were visible.

🧠 Analysis

Scene complexity had a measurable impact on performance.
Simpler geometries (FR1_RPY) produced stable meshes with low RMSE, whereas cluttered indoor scenes (FR1_Room) reduced both accuracy and speed.
Even with discrete GPU acceleration, real-time operation was not achieved.
The bottleneck occurred during voxel integration and surface fusion, confirming the trade-off between reconstruction precision and computational speed in volumetric mapping.

🧭 Reflection

This task provided hands-on understanding of dense SLAM and the computational limits of real-time 3D vision.
Reconstructing multiple datasets reinforced concepts in:

  • RGB-D frame alignment and TSDF fusion
  • Hardware–software performance trade-offs
  • Evaluation metrics (FPS / RMSE)
  • Visual inspection of mesh completeness

While the results achieved high fidelity for smaller environments, scaling to larger or dynamic scenes remains an open research challenge without dedicated GPU hardware or algorithmic optimization.

“Precision and Performance constantly trade places when turning motion into mapped reality.”
entry.summary: Experimented with KinectFusion using RGB-D data from the TUM dataset to perform 3D reconstruction, analyze performance metrics, and evaluate limitations in complex scenes.
